params.question: Which unique feature of the olfactory pathway distinguishes it from all other sensory pathways to the cerebral cortex?

answers.text: It uses only unmyelinated C fibres for conduction

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While olfactory nerve fibres are indeed unmyelinated, this is not the defining distinction. The key feature is that olfactory signals reach the primary olfactory cortex without synapsing in the thalamus — a direct limbic connection that explains why smell triggers vivid emotional memories.

answers.text: It bypasses the thalamus and projects directly to the cortex

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The olfactory pathway is the only sensory pathway that reaches the cortex without relaying through the thalamus. Signals travel from the olfactory bulb directly to the primary olfactory cortex and limbic system, which is why smell is so powerfully linked to emotion and memory.

answers.text: It decussates completely at the level of the brainstem

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The olfactory pathway does not undergo complete brainstem decussation. Its unique feature is bypassing the thalamus entirely — olfactory signals reach the primary olfactory cortex and limbic structures directly, unlike all other sensory modalities.

answers.text: It is carried by the trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Olfaction is carried by cranial nerve I (the olfactory nerve), not CN V. The trigeminal nerve carries irritant sensations such as ammonia from the nasal mucosa — which is precisely why ammonia must be avoided when testing the sense of smell clinically.

overallFeedback.feedback: The olfactory pathway is unique because it reaches the cortex without passing through the thalamus. This direct limbic connection explains why smells trigger powerful emotional memories.
Well done. The direct cortical projection without a thalamic relay is the hallmark of the olfactory pathway and explains its strong emotional associations.

interactions.label: Which structures in the inner ear are responsible for detecting rotational head

params.question: Which structures in the inner ear are responsible for detecting rotational head movements?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The utricle and saccule are otolith organs that detect linear acceleration and the pull of gravity — such as during head tilt or riding in a lift. Rotational (angular) head movements are detected by the three semicircular canals, which are oriented in different planes.

Correct. The three semicircular canals are oriented in three perpendicular planes and detect rotational (angular) head movements. The otolith organs — the utricle and saccule — serve a different function, detecting linear acceleration and gravity. Together, they provide the brain with a complete picture of head position and movement.

answers.text: Organ of Corti on the basilar membrane

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The organ of Corti is the sensory receptor for hearing, not balance. It sits on the basilar membrane within the cochlea and converts sound vibrations into nerve signals. Rotational movements are detected by the semicircular canals of the vestibular apparatus.

The ossicular chain transmits and amplifies sound vibrations from the tympanic membrane to the oval window of the cochlea. It is part of the hearing apparatus, not the balance system. Rotational head movements are detected by the semicircular canals.

overallFeedback.feedback: The three semicircular canals detect rotational head movements. They work alongside the otolith organs (utricle and saccule), which detect linear acceleration and gravity, to maintain balance and spatial orientation.
Exactly right. The semicircular canals detect rotation, while the otolith organs detect linear acceleration and gravity — two complementary systems within the vestibular apparatus.

params.question: A patient with a pituitary tumour compressing the optic chiasma from below develops which characteristic visual field defect?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Homonymous hemianopia results from lesions BEYOND the chiasma — in the optic tract, lateral geniculate body, or visual cortex. A pituitary tumour compresses the chiasma itself, specifically damaging the crossing nasal fibres from both eyes, producing a different pattern.

Correct. A pituitary tumour presses on the optic chiasma from below, damaging the crossing nasal fibres from both eyes. These nasal fibres carry information from the temporal visual fields, so their interruption produces bitemporal hemianopia — loss of both temporal (outer) visual fields.

Binasal hemianopia would require bilateral damage to the temporal (non-crossing) fibres at the chiasma — an extremely rare pattern. A pituitary tumour compresses the CROSSING nasal fibres from below, producing bitemporal hemianopia, not binasal.

Bilateral central scotomas suggest optic nerve or macular pathology, not chiasmal compression. A pituitary tumour pressing the chiasma from below selectively damages the crossing nasal fibres, producing the classic bitemporal hemianopia pattern.

overallFeedback.feedback: A pituitary tumour compresses the optic chiasma from below, damaging the crossing nasal fibres from both eyes. Since nasal fibres carry temporal visual field information, the result is bitemporal hemianopia.
Exactly right. The nasal fibres cross at the chiasma; a pituitary tumour below compresses them selectively, producing the classic bitemporal hemianopia.

interactions.label: Deficiency of which vitamin impairs rhodopsin regeneration in rod photoreceptors

params.question: Deficiency of which vitamin impairs rhodopsin regeneration in rod photoreceptors and causes night blindness (nyctalopia)?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Vitamin B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia and peripheral neuropathy, not night blindness. Rhodopsin regeneration in rods specifically requires vitamin A (retinol), which is converted to retinal — the light-sensitive chromophore component of rhodopsin.

Correct. Vitamin A (retinol) is converted to 11-cis-retinal, the light-sensitive chromophore in rhodopsin. Without adequate vitamin A, rods cannot regenerate rhodopsin after it is bleached by light, and dark adaptation fails — resulting in night blindness (nyctalopia).

Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy through impaired collagen synthesis, not visual problems. Rod photoreceptors require vitamin A for rhodopsin regeneration. Without it, dark adaptation is impaired and night vision fails.

Vitamin D deficiency affects calcium metabolism and causes rickets or osteomalacia, not visual deficits. Night blindness results from vitamin A deficiency, which prevents rhodopsin regeneration during the rod phase of dark adaptation.

overallFeedback.feedback: Vitamin A is required for regeneration of rhodopsin, the visual pigment in rods. Its deficiency impairs dark adaptation and causes night blindness (nyctalopia).
Correct. Vitamin A is essential for rhodopsin regeneration — its deficiency remains one of the leading preventable causes of blindness worldwide.
